title: Sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:30–44)
hookLine: he looks at the crowd with compassion and feeds five thousand

cards: The twelve come back from their travels full of stories, and exhausted. So many people are coming and going that they don't even have time to eat. Jesus says, come away with me to a quiet place and rest a while.
They get in the boat. The crowd sees, runs around the shore on foot, and gets there first. The boat lands, and there they are.
Thousands. The day off is gone before it starts. Mark tells us what Jesus felt.

teach.b: In the old King James Bible, Jesus "saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd."

Moved with compassion is a gut word in Greek, about the insides: compassion felt deep in the body. And sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase in Israel's scriptures for a people with no one to guide or protect them.
So he teaches them many things, until the day is far spent. Then it's late, and the disciples do the sensible thing: send them away to buy food.
Jesus answers: "Give ye them to eat." You give them something. They do the math out loud: should they go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread?
He asks, what have you got? Five loaves and two fish. He has everyone sit in groups on the grass.
Mark notices it was green, which some read as a hint of spring. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out.
Take, bless, break, give: Christian readers hear those same four actions again at the Last Supper, and at the communion table today.
Everyone eats and is satisfied, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Some readers smile that there's one for each disciple who said send them away.
About five thousand men, Mark says; Matthew adds, besides women and children. Christians have read it as a miracle of Jesus's power and a picture of God feeding his people.
Some also notice he didn't let the disciples off the hook. He started with their little and put it in their hands.

how: Many Christians connect the feeding of the five thousand with communion, where bread is blessed, broken and given, and churches often run food banks and shared meals with this story in mind.

games.q: you wanted a day off. the crowd got there first, it's late, and there's no food. you're a disciple. what do you suggest?
o: send them away to buy food.
ask the crowd to go home and come back tomorrow.
games.why: they say send them away. Jesus answers: give ye them to eat, and turns their five loaves and two fish into enough.

practice: Picture a crowd you'll be part of, a commute, a store, a waiting room; a crowd can feel like an obstacle. Try seeing it the way the text says Jesus did: tired faces, hungry ones, some with no one looking out for them.
If you pray, you can pray for that crowd, and ask what little you have that could go into someone's hands.

wordCard.voice: Compassion, the gut-deep feeling, in Greek, behind Jesus seeing a tired crowd not as a nuisance but as sheep without a shepherd.
